properties.name: Hou Hanshu eclipse of 31 CE — Luoyang court
properties.found: Channel claims Later Han annals record an "impossible" eclipse, the phrase "man from heaven died", and the emperor taking the people's sins on himself, around the crucifixion (dated by the video to 3 April 33).
properties.support: Hou Hanshu, Guangwu annals, Jianwu 7 (31 CE): 三月癸亥晦，日有食之 — on the last day (guihai) of the 3rd month the sun was eclipsed. On the eclipse day the emperor left the main hall and issued a self-blame edict (吾德薄致災 — my thin virtue brought this disaster). A later edict (summer, 4th month, renwu day) says: 比陰陽錯謬，日月薄食。百姓有過，在予一人 — lately yin and yang have gone wrong and the sun and moon have been eclipsed; if the people have faults, the blame is on me, the one man. It then grants a general amnesty. The Chinese date (last day of the 3rd month) matches the annular solar eclipse of 10 May 31 CE — not a Passover date and not the crucifixion darkness.
properties.notes: Rating: MISLEADING. The eclipse (a real solar eclipse, 10 May 31 CE) and the edict exist, but the date is 31 not 33; "the people's faults rest on me" is a stock formula of Chinese royal self-blame (from the Analects 20.1 堯曰 and the Shangshu), not atonement theology; the "man from heaven died" line was not found in the annals.
properties.caveat: Verify full annal text on ctext before wiring; "rainbow halo" claim not checked.

recent_updates.title: New video: 上帝 Shàngdì as an ancient Chinese name for God
recent_updates.text: The creator remembers saying 上帝 Shàngdì, the word many Chinese Protestant churches use for God, and argues that the name was used in China long before Christianity arrived. He presents this as a link to the biblical God.
recent_updates.caveat: Shangdi appears in Shang oracle bones (c. 1250–1050 BCE), mostly as 帝 Di; the full form 上帝 is common in the Shijing and Shangshu, so the “3,500 years” figure is generous. Some Christians see Shangdi as an echo of early knowledge of the one Creator; scholars see him as the high god of Shang and Zhou religion, alongside ancestor worship. This is a comparison, not the same as YHWH. 上帝 was later chosen by Protestant translators for “God” in Chinese Bibles (Catholics mostly use 天主 Tiānzhǔ), so the church word comes from that translation choice.

properties.name: St Thomas Mount & San Thome Basilica, Chennai
properties.found: A YouTube channel (@japhetsworld) presents the tradition that the apostle Thomas reached India about AD 52, converted families in Kerala and was martyred near Chennai in AD 72.
properties.support: Cosmas Indicopleustes (Christian Topography, Book 3, c. 550) reports a church in Malê, 'where the pepper grows' (the translator identifies it as Malabar), and a bishop appointed from Persia at another place called Calliana. He also reports a church with clergy on Taprobanê (Ceylon). The Acts of Thomas, a Syriac work surviving also in Greek, tells how Thomas was sold as a carpenter to Abbanes, a merchant sent by King Gundaphorus (Gudnaphar), went to India, and was later killed with spears under a king named Misdaeus (Syriac Mazdai).
properties.notes: Rating: TRADITION, PARTLY SUPPORTED. Christians in India, with a bishop appointed from Persia, are attested by about AD 550 (Cosmas). Thomas's personal mission to India is an ancient tradition, known from the apocryphal Acts of Thomas; Encyclopaedia Iranica notes that he reputedly went to Madras, where a church is named in his honour. Gondophares was a real Indo-Parthian king: the British Museum holds his coins (e.g., IOC.231, found at Begram, dated c. AD 32-60, naming him in Greek and Kharoshthi). The so-called Takht-i-Bahi inscription is dated in the 26th regnal year of maharaja Guduvhara (Gondophares) and year 103 of an era (Konow, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum II.1, 1929, pp. 57-62). It was actually found at nearby Shahbazgarhi. Iranica reads the era as the Vikrama era, giving AD 46 and a reign of about AD 20-46. Rienjang notes the era is unspecified on the stone.
properties.caveat: Pin at San Thome (burial tradition); St Thomas Mount ~10 km SW.

Interpretation: the video argues from weathering that the Sphinx may be about 12,000 years old; AERA dates it to Khafre.

recent_updates.title: Video: an older Sphinx from weathering? (claim assessed)
recent_updates.text: The host explains why he studied limestone weathering on old gravestones and quarry walls, and argues that the weathering of the Sphinx and its enclosure points to heavy rainfall and sheet floods, so the monument may be far older than the Old Kingdom. He repeats a proposal that about 12,000 years ago the Sphinx faced the constellation Leo rising at the spring equinox.
recent_updates.caveat: AERA (Mark Lehner) dates the Sphinx to Khafre (Greek Chephren), late in his reign in the 4th Dynasty, about 4,500 years ago: Lehner’s stone-by-stone mapping matched the Sphinx Temple’s core blocks to the layers quarried from the Sphinx ditch. The older-Sphinx view comes from a minority of geologists (Robert Schoch, 1992), and AERA names and rejects it. The Leo/equinox alignment is an astronomical argument, not dating evidence. No link to any biblical event; Giza is a context pin only.

properties.name: Behbeit el-Hagar (بهبيت الحجارة) — Ramesses II colossal statues
properties.found: A rescue excavation by Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, prompted by a villager’s inscribed granite block, found fragments of two colossal royal statues on the western side of the temple complex. One, a 1.6 m head in the Double Crown with a back-pillar inscription, is identified as Ramesses II; the second, a 2.4 m fragment wearing the nemes headcloth, is probably the same king.
properties.support: Egyptian context only. Scripture never names the Exodus pharaoh.
properties.notes: The ministry reports royal titles on the back pillar and the granite block (a Horus name, “King of Upper and Lower Egypt”, “Son of Ra”). The king’s throne and birth names are not reported as read on these blocks. The standing Isis temple here is mostly Nectanebo II (360–343 BCE) and Ptolemaic; the Ramesses II pieces point to earlier building.
caveats: Scripture never names the Exodus pharaoh; this find makes no biblical link.
Work is ongoing; no publication yet.

claims.strength_reason: Exodus 1–14 calls the king only 'Pharaoh' and never gives his name. The cited Smithsonian report describes Ramses II colossi found at Behbeit El-Hagar in the Nile Delta and makes no Exodus link, so 'Egyptian context only' is accurate. Weakness: none for the claim as worded; it is a caution, not evidence.
